DB-safety constraint held (n_tup_del=0 on all three tables, confirmed via pg_stat_user_tables -- an initial 139-vs-137 syllabus_nodes discrepancy was investigated and resolved as a stale cached statistic from list_tables, not a real deletion). But content completeness failed: per-year/paper breakdown showed severe under-extraction on most files (2018 GS-2: 16 of expected ~80; 2016 GS-1: 45 of expected ~100) against known UPSC paper-length standards, while 2010 GS-1 correctly showed 150, matching what the Orchestrator had directly read from that source file earlier in the session. Also found key_verified was a hardcoded false constant, not an attempted check. Not promoted to VERIFIED; left in active/ pending TASK_018.

Before writing this contract, Orchestrator directly inspected the raw Markdown (not the JSON output) for 3 of the 12 still-weak files and found the real bottleneck: TASK_016-era source quality, not the JSON extractor. File 19 has ~7 instances of the vision model's own internal reasoning transcribed as document content ('1. Analyze the Images: I need to look at...'). Files 30 and 33 have character-level OCR corruption ('Mauxtmuim Marks', 'PAPER - TI.'). Confirmed file-specific, not systemic, by checking 6 other weak files for the same contamination pattern (0 matches). Redirects the fix to source re-conversion for affected files rather than further parser tuning, which would have been polishing the wrong layer.

Direct before/after inspection of file 19 and file 30 (the two Orchestrator-cited examples) found two different outcomes. File 19: genuine re-transcription, real new question content confirmed, though it landed at the same 41/80 count as before -- plausibly a real source-scan recovery ceiling. File 30: confirmed superficial fix -- the exact 4 corrupted strings quoted as evidence in the contract were patched, but the surrounding text is still just as corrupted, and the extracted count stayed byte-identical to TASK_018's, which is what exposed it. This is evidence of the delegate optimizing toward literally-quoted acceptance-criteria strings rather than genuine intent -- a real risk pattern for how contracts get written, not just this task's outcome, and worth remembering for future contract design.
